en.g: Report questions correctly with normal word order and no question mark.
p: Wh- questions: Where do you live? becomes He asked me where I lived. No do/does/did, normal order.
Yes/no questions use if or whether: Are you ready? becomes She asked if I was ready.
Tenses move back as in statements: Can you help? becomes He asked if I could help.

en.g: Report more precisely with verbs like suggest, promise, refuse and remind.
p: Verb + to: promise, refuse, offer, agree. He promised to call. She offered to help. They refused to wait.

Suggest + -ing or suggest that: He suggested going to the beach. Explain + that: She explained that...

en.g: Share news you heard in a natural, friendly way.
p: Openers: Guess what! Did you hear about...? You'll never guess what happened!

en.c: Share three pieces of good news in English, each with a different opener, and add one reaction for each.

en.t: Modal deduction: must be, can't be
en.g: Make logical guesses about the present with must, might and can't.
p: Must = I'm almost sure it's true: She must be at work. Her car isn't here. You must be tired after that trip.
Can't = I'm almost sure it's false: That can't be Tom, he's in Rome. It can't be so late already!
Might, may, could = maybe: He might be in a meeting. It could be the delivery at the door.
en.q: Your friend isn't answering the phone. Make three guesses with must, might and can't.
en.c: Look around you and write five deductions: That must be..., This can't be..., She might be...

p: Must = fast sicher wahr: She must be at work. Her car isn't here. You must be tired after that trip.
Can't = fast sicher falsch: That can't be Tom, he's in Rome. It can't be so late already!
Might, may, could = vielleicht: He might be in a meeting. It could be the delivery at the door.

en.g: Guess about the past with modal + have + past participle.
p: Must have = almost sure: They must have left early. The lights are off. You must have worked hard.
Might have / could have = maybe: He might have missed the bus. She could have forgotten.
Can't have = almost sure it didn't happen: She can't have seen us. She didn't wave.

en.g: Use the passive in many tenses: present perfect, continuous and future.
p: Present perfect: has/have been + participle. The bridge has been built. My order has been sent.
Continuous: is/was being + participle. The road is being repaired. The room was being cleaned.
Future and modals: will be / can be + participle. It will be finished soon. Tickets can be bought online.

en.c: Write one passive sentence in each tense: is made, was made, has been made, is being made, will be made.

p: Present Perfect: has/have been + Partizip. The bridge has been built. My order has been sent.
Verlaufsform: is/was being + Partizip. The road is being repaired. The room was being cleaned.
Zukunft und Modalverben: will be / can be + Partizip. It will be finished soon. Tickets can be bought online.

en.g: Understand when relative clauses need commas and when they don't.
p: Defining: no commas, the information is essential. The man who lives next door is a pilot.
Non-defining: commas, extra information. My brother, who lives in Lima, is a pilot. I have only one brother.
In non-defining clauses, use who or which, never that: Our car, which is red, is very old.
en.q: Tell me about a person or place you love, adding extra information with who or which between commas.
en.c: Write three defining and three non-defining sentences about your family, city and favourite things.

In Sätzen mit Kommas nur who oder which, nie that: Our car, which is red, is very old.

en.g: Use which after a comma to comment on a whole idea.
p: Which can refer to the whole sentence: He passed all his exams, which was amazing.
Great for comments and feelings: The train was late, which meant we missed the start.
